newsitem.title: USA: Fed sees growing economy, muted inflation in Nov.
newsitem.headline: Fed sees growing economy, muted inflation in Nov.

text.p: The economy kept growing moderately during November with little or no sign of wage and price pressures flaring up, the Federal Reserve said Wednesday.

Skilled employees were in short supply across the country yet there was no acceleration in wage demands while retail prices remained stable despite more costly raw materials, the latest Beige Book summary of economic activity said.
Retail sales were on the upswing and most storeowners were "modestly optimistic" that the holiday shopping period through Christmas would be a bountiful one for merchants.

"Moderate economic growth continues to be reported in nearly all Federal Reserve districts," the summary prepared by the Philadelphia Fed concluded. It was based on interviews with businessmen in all 12 Fed districts done before Nov 23.
The Beige Book will be used by central bank policymakers when the Federal Open Market Committee gathers on Dec 17 to plot interest-rate strategy at their final session this year.
The last Beige Book, issued on Oct 30, similarly noted tight labor markets. But the latest Fed summary said strong hiring and shortages did not seem to be translating into big wage demands.

"Reports ... do not indicate a generalized acceleration in wage increases despite growing reports of labor shortages," the central bank summary said. Skilled trades workers and specialized technical employees were reported in particularly short supply.
Retailers in the Boston, New York and Phildelphia Fed regions were anticipating gains in holiday sales ranging from two percent to six percent over last year.
"In St. Louis, Kansas City, Dallas and San Francisco the season is expected to be strong," the regional Fed banks reported.

Many retailers do half their yearly business in the few weeks between Thanksgiving and Christmas so retail sales are being closely scrutinized since consumer spending fuels two-thirds of national economic activity.
The Fed summary said there has been "virtually no change" in retail prices in recent weeks. There was some firming in raw materials costs and in prices for intermediate goods.
The regional Fed banks in Richmond, Va, as well as in Atlanta, Kansas City and Dallas said there manufacturing and construction material costs were on the rise.

Manufacturing activity kept growing during October and November. Most said the pickup was modest, though the Boston Fed said manufacturers there were reporting gains of up to 15 percent in their orders and revenues.

In the past four weeks, retail sales were stronger nearly across the country, with the pickup ranging from higher clothing sales in New York, Cleveland, Atlanta and Dallas to more sales of home products in Atlanta and St Louis.
New-car sales were steady in most districts, according to auto dealers, with the sole negative report coming from Dallas where sales were characterized as sluggish, the Fed said.
